static.topic: Air Quality Governance in India: NCAP, GRAP and CAQM
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Pollution and Environmental Governance
static.whatIsIt: India's air pollution response rests on the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the CPCB, supplemented by the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) for city-level targets and the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) for emergency curbs in the Delhi-NCR region.
static.background: The CPCB was constituted in 1974 under the Water Act and later entrusted with air pollution regulation. The Supreme Court, in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, drove the creation of an emergency action plan for Delhi, and GRAP was notified in 2017 on the direction of the Supreme Court by the EPCA. The Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas (CAQM) was set up by ordinance in 2020 and given statutory backing by the CAQM Act, 2021, taking over GRAP implementation and revising it in 2022. NCAP was launched in 2019 with an initial target of a 20–30% reduction in PM10 and PM2.5 by 2024 over 2017 levels, later revised to a 40% cut in PM10 by 2025-26 across non-attainment cities.
static.geography: The Delhi-NCR sits in the Indo-Gangetic Plain, where winter temperature inversion, calm winds, low mixing height and the Himalayan barrier trap pollutants close to the ground, sharply worsening AQI from late October to January.
static.socioEconomic: Pollution episodes impose health expenditure, lost workdays and productivity losses; the burden falls disproportionately on outdoor workers, the elderly, children and low-income households with limited access to clean-air alternatives.
static.whyInNews: Delhi's AQI has remained in the 'very poor' category, keeping GRAP-stage restrictions and political debate over the effectiveness of NCAP and CAQM alive.
static.wayForward: Strengthen source-apportionment-based action, expand continuous ambient monitoring beyond metros, enforce sector-specific emission norms, integrate air-quality management with urban transport, energy and waste policy, and build a transparent, time-bound accountability framework for NCAP targets.
prelimsPointers: The National AQI, launched in 2015 by the CPCB, is computed from eight pollutants — PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, NH3, O3 and Pb — and has six categories from 'Good' to 'Severe'.
GRAP has four stages: Stage I 'Poor' (AQI 201–300), Stage II 'Very Poor' (301–400), Stage III 'Severe' (401–450) and Stage IV 'Severe Plus' (above 450).
India's NAAQS (2009) permit PM2.5 of 40 µg/m³ annually and 60 µg/m³ over 24 hours, far above the WHO 2021 guideline values of 5 µg/m³ and 15 µg/m³ respectively.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether India's command-and-control, emergency-driven air quality framework can deliver durable reductions in particulate pollution, or whether it needs to be replaced by a source-based, fiscally backed and legally enforceable clean air regime.

static.topic: Health Burden of Air Pollution and India's Welfare Response
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare, Health and Rights
static.whatIsIt: India's welfare architecture combines rights-based legislation with DBT-enabled delivery through the JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) backbone; in health, Ayushman Bharat (2018) has an insurance arm, PM-JAY, alongside Health and Wellness Centres, while private health insurance increasingly absorbs pollution-linked claims.
static.background: Rights-based laws such as MGNREGA (2005), the RTE Act (2009) and the National Food Security Act (2013) established entitlement-based welfare. Ayushman Bharat, launched in 2018, added a health-insurance and primary-care layer. The Supreme Court has read the right to a clean environment into Article 21, and Article 48A (DPSP) and Article 51A(g) (fundamental duty) place environmental protection within the constitutional scheme.
static.socioEconomic: Rising pollution-related insurance claims signal a shift of the health cost of pollution onto households and insurers, with working professionals and senior citizens most affected; this compounds out-of-pocket expenditure and can push vulnerable families into distress.
static.whyInNews: A report cited by The Hindu BusinessLine says pollution-related health insurance claims rose 4.3 times in three years, with Delhi leading among cities.
static.wayForward: Integrate air-quality data with health surveillance and insurance actuarial models, expand PM-JAY and primary-care capacity for respiratory and cardiovascular illness, and treat clean air as a public-health entitlement rather than an episodic emergency.
prelimsPointers: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per year.
Four labour codes consolidate 29 existing labour laws.
Ayushman Bharat (2018) has two components: PM-JAY for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation, and Health and Wellness Centres for primary care.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how environmental degradation is becoming a welfare and public-health challenge, and assess whether India's health financing architecture is equipped to absorb pollution-induced morbidity.

static.topic: Winter Pollution in the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the Right to Clean Air
static.syllabusNode: Geography — Physical Geography, Climate and Environmental Geography
static.whatIsIt: The Indo-Gangetic Plain experiences a recurring winter pollution trap created by the interaction of meteorology — temperature inversion, low wind speed, shallow mixing height — with dense emissions from transport, industry, construction, waste burning and agricultural residue burning.
static.background: Post-monsoon stubble burning in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh coincides with the onset of winter inversion over north India, producing the sharpest AQI deterioration of the year. The Supreme Court has repeatedly intervened on Delhi's air quality, and the EPCA-era GRAP was the first structured emergency response, later taken over and revised by CAQM.
static.geography: The Himalayas to the north block the dispersal of pollutants, while the plain's topography and winter atmospheric stability prevent vertical mixing; the result is a persistent aerosol layer over northern India visible in satellite imagery each November–January.
static.socioEconomic: Agricultural residue burning is tied to short crop-rotation windows and the economics of residue management, making it a farm-livelihood question as much as an environmental one.
static.whyInNews: Delhi's AQI has stayed in the 'very poor' band, sustaining the annual winter pollution crisis and the political contestation around it.
static.wayForward: Combine crop-residue management incentives with diversified cropping patterns, strengthen regional (not just city-level) airshed management across NCR states, and align transport, power and industrial policy with airshed-level emission caps.
prelimsPointers: Temperature inversion in winter traps cooler, denser air with pollutants near the surface, preventing vertical dispersion.
Air pollution is a transboundary, airshed-level problem: emissions in one state affect AQI across the entire Indo-Gangetic Plain.
static.mainsAngle: Explain the meteorological and anthropogenic factors behind north India's winter pollution episodes, and examine why airshed-level coordination is essential to any durable solution.

prelims: The National AQI (CPCB, 2015) uses eight pollutants and six categories; 'Very Poor' corresponds to AQI 301–400 and 'Severe' to 401–500.
GRAP, first notified in 2017 on Supreme Court direction and revised by CAQM in 2022, has four stages of escalating restrictions tied to AQI thresholds.
NCAP (2019) initially targeted a 20–30% reduction in PM10 and PM2.5 by 2024 over 2017 levels, later revised to a 40% cut in PM10 by 2025-26 for non-attainment cities.
India's NAAQS (2009) allow PM2.5 of 40 µg/m³ (annual) and 60 µg/m³ (24-hour), well above the WHO 2021 guidelines of 5 µg/m³ and 15 µg/m³.
stories.mainsQuestion: Air pollution in India is increasingly being measured not only in AQI terms but also in health expenditure and insurance claims. Examine the adequacy of India's existing legal and institutional framework for air quality management, and suggest reforms to make clean air a enforceable public-health entitlement.

stories.headline: Italy fines Meta €805 million over Android users' data access
stories.summary: Italy's competition regulator has imposed a fine of €805 million (about $887 million) on Meta, accusing the company of failing to inform roughly 20 million users that it had access to their photos and other data on Android devices. The penalty, reported on 14 November 2026, is a penalty of a scale rarely seen from a national regulator in Europe against a technology platform. Reuters frames the action around Android users' data access, while the BBC foregrounds the photo-access disclosure failure affecting some 20 million users. The case adds to a widening set of European proceedings against large platforms over consent, data linking and market power.
stories.whyItMatters: It illustrates the global shift from ex-post antitrust action to ex-ante and privacy-based regulation of Big Tech, a template India is actively debating through the DPDP Act and proposals for a digital competition law.

static.topic: EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and cross-border data enforcement
static.syllabusNode: Important aspects of governance, transparency and accountability; international institutions and agreements affecting India's interests
static.whatIsIt: The GDPR is the European Union's comprehensive data protection regulation governing the processing of personal data of individuals in the EU/EEA. It rests on principles such as lawfulness, purpose limitation, data minimisation and consent, and is enforced by national supervisory authorities coordinated through a one-stop-shop mechanism.
static.background: Adopted in 2016 and applicable from 25 May 2018, the GDPR replaced the 1995 Data Protection Directive. It created a single set of rules across the EU, gave individuals rights such as access, erasure and portability, and empowered regulators to levy administrative fines of up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher. National regulators such as Italy's competition and data authorities have since acted against large platforms over consent and data-linking practices.
static.geography: European Union and European Economic Area; applies extraterritorially to organisations outside the EU that process EU residents' data.
static.socioEconomic: Compliance costs weigh heavily on smaller firms, while enforcement against large platforms shapes the global template for data governance and influences India's own data protection debate.
static.whyInNews: Italy's €805 million penalty on Meta over access to users' photos and data without adequate disclosure is a fresh example of national-level enforcement under Europe's data protection architecture.
static.wayForward: Greater consistency in cross-border enforcement, clearer consent design standards, and interoperability between EU and third-country data regimes to reduce compliance fragmentation.
prelimsPointers: GDPR became applicable on 25 May 2018, replacing the 1995 Data Protection Directive.
Maximum GDPR penalty is €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.
GDPR has extraterritorial reach over entities processing EU residents' personal data.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the GDPR's enforcement model balances individual privacy rights against innovation and compliance burdens, and what lessons it holds for India's data protection regime.

static.topic: Ex-ante regulation of Big Tech: the EU Digital Markets Act and gatekeepers
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — competition, market regulation and regulatory institutions; effects of liberalisation on the economy
static.whatIsIt: The Digital Markets Act (DMA) is an EU regulation that designates large online platforms as 'gatekeepers' and imposes a list of do's and don'ts on them — including restrictions on self-preferencing, combining personal data across services, and anti-steering practices — before any abuse is proven.
static.background: Proposed in December 2020 and adopted in 2022, the DMA became applicable from 2 May 2023, with the first gatekeeper designations announced in September 2023 covering major platforms including Meta. It complements the Digital Services Act, which governs content and platform accountability. The DMA marks a shift from case-by-case antitrust enforcement to ex-ante rule-making for digital markets.
static.geography: European Union single market; obligations apply to designated gatekeepers operating in the EU irrespective of their country of origin.
static.socioEconomic: Aimed at improving contestability and fairness for business users and consumers, but criticised by platforms as raising compliance costs and by some economists as potentially chilling innovation.
static.whyInNews: The Italian penalty on Meta over Android data access sits within the broader European push to regulate platform conduct through both competition and data protection tools.
static.wayForward: Effective enforcement capacity, clear compliance metrics, and international regulatory coordination to prevent forum shopping by global platforms.
prelimsPointers: The DMA became applicable from 2 May 2023; first gatekeeper designations were made in September 2023.
Gatekeeper designation thresholds include EU turnover of at least €7.5 billion or market capitalisation of at least €75 billion, plus 45 million monthly active end users.
DMA penalties can reach 10% of global turnover, rising to 20% for repeat infringements.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether ex-ante regulation of digital markets is a more effective response to platform dominance than traditional ex-post antitrust enforcement.

static.topic: India's data protection and digital competition framework
static.syllabusNode: Government policies and interventions for development in various sectors; Fundamental Rights — Right to Privacy
static.whatIsIt: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is the country's first comprehensive data protection statute, built on consent-based processing, data principal rights and obligations for data fiduciaries, and enforced by a Data Protection Board of India. In parallel, the Competition Commission of India regulates abuse of dominance in digital markets under the Competition Act, 2002.
static.background: Privacy was recognised as a fundamental right under Article 21 in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017). The Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee (2017–18) recommended a data protection framework; the Personal Data Protection Bill, 2019 was withdrawn in 2022 and replaced by the DPDP Act, which received presidential assent in August 2023. Separately, the CCI penalised Google in 2022 in the Android case, and the Committee on Digital Competition Law submitted its report in 2024 recommending a dedicated digital competition law.
static.geography: India; the DPDP Act also has extraterritorial application to processing of personal data outside India in certain circumstances.
static.socioEconomic: Balancing citizen privacy, the compliance burden on startups, and the market power of large platforms is central to India's digital economy policy.
static.whyInNews: Italy's action against Meta over undisclosed data access highlights the enforcement questions India will face as the DPDP Act's rules are operationalised and digital competition law is debated.
static.wayForward: Timely notification of DPDP rules, an independent and well-resourced Data Protection Board, and a calibrated ex-ante digital competition framework that avoids over-regulation of emerging firms.
prelimsPointers: The DPDP Act, 2023 received presidential assent in August 2023 and establishes a Data Protection Board of India.
The CCI penalised Google in 2022 in the Android mobile operating system case for abuse of dominance.
The Committee on Digital Competition Law (report submitted 2024) recommended a separate Digital Competition Act for ex-ante regulation.
static.mainsAngle: Critically examine whether India's existing competition and data protection framework is adequate to regulate the conduct of large digital platforms, and suggest reforms.

prelims: Italy's competition regulator fined Meta €805 million (about $887 million) on 14 November 2026 over access to users' data on Android devices.
The allegation centres on Meta failing to inform roughly 20 million users that it had access to their photos.
Italy's antitrust authority is the Autorità Garante della Concorrenza e del Mercato (AGCM), which enforces both competition and certain consumer protection rules.
The action adds to a series of European regulatory proceedings against large technology platforms over consent, data linking and market conduct.
stories.mainsQuestion: Large digital platforms now face both ex-post antitrust action and ex-ante, privacy-based regulation across jurisdictions. Examine the implications of such regulatory action for competition, innovation and user rights, and suggest an appropriate regulatory framework for India.

It also reinforces the pattern of courts intervening when statutory and autonomous bodies are accused of procedural lapses in high-stakes public examinations.

static.topic: Judicial Review and the Writ Jurisdiction of High Courts
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: Supreme Court, High Courts and Judicial Review
static.whatIsIt: Judicial review is the power of courts to test executive action and legislation against the Constitution. High Courts exercise this power under Article 226, issuing writs to enforce fundamental rights and 'for any other purpose', a scope wider than the Supreme Court's Article 32 jurisdiction.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC) provide writ jurisdiction.
static.socioEconomic: Judicial intervention in examination and recruitment processes affects lakhs of aspirants' careers and the credibility of public recruitment institutions.

static.wayForward: Strengthen internal grievance-redressal and expert re-verification mechanisms within examination agencies so that key disputes are resolved before litigation; courts can then confine themselves to reviewing procedural fairness rather than re-evaluating academic content.

static.topic: UGC-NET and the National Testing Agency

The National Testing Agency was set up in 2017 as an autonomous society to conduct entrance and eligibility examinations, taking over the conduct of UGC-NET from the CBSE. Answer keys are published after the exam with a window for candidates to raise objections, following which an expert committee finalises the key.
static.socioEconomic: UGC-NET results determine teaching eligibility and research fellowships, directly shaping academic employment and higher-education research capacity.
static.whyInNews: The Delhi High Court has ordered a review of four answer key entries of UGC-NET, raising questions about the reliability of the key-finalisation process.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise a transparent, time-bound expert review of challenged keys with published reasoning, and build in independent audit of question-setting and moderation.

NTA, set up in 2017, conducts UGC-NET.
UGC-NET qualifies candidates for Assistant Professor and JRF.

stories.headline: Kerala High Court suggests lowering juvenile age limit to 16
stories.summary: The Kerala High Court, while hearing a matter, reportedly observed that the age of juvenility should be brought down from 18 to 16, according to legal news outlet Bar & Bench. The observation revives a long-running debate over whether adolescents in the 16–18 bracket who commit grave offences should be dealt with under the protective framework of the Juvenile Justice Act or tried as adults. Under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, a 'child' is anyone below 18, though the Juvenile Justice Board may allow 16–18 year olds accused of heinous offences to be tried as adults. Since the age threshold is set by statute, any change would require legislative action by Parliament rather than a judicial direction. The remark is therefore best read as a judicial nudge to the legislature, not a binding ruling.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the constitutional boundary between judicial observation and legislative policy, and directly touches the reformative philosophy of India's juvenile justice law — a recurring GS-II theme on child rights, deterrence versus rehabilitation, and the age of criminal responsibility.

perspectives.take: A court-reporting outlet framing the development as a judicial suggestion to reduce the juvenile age limit to 16, with emphasis on the High Court's observation rather than on legislative or child-rights counterarguments.

static.topic: High Courts and Judicial Review (Articles 214, 226)
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary
static.whatIsIt: High Courts are the apex judicial authorities at the state level, established under Article 214, with writ jurisdiction under Article 226 and the power of judicial review over legislative and executive action.
static.background: High Courts trace their origin to the Indian High Courts Act, 1861, and were continued under Articles 214–231 of the Constitution. Judicial review flows from Articles 13, 32 and 226, and the basic-structure doctrine was laid down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973). The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998), and PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s.
static.whyInNews: The Kerala High Court's reported suggestion to lower the juvenile age limit to 16 illustrates how courts flag perceived gaps in legislative policy, even where the subject lies within Parliament's domain.
static.wayForward: Courts may highlight deficiencies, but the age of juvenility is a legislative policy choice; any change should follow wide consultation, data on offending in the 16–18 age group, and assessment of Juvenile Justice Board capacity.
prelimsPointers: Article 214 provides for a High Court for each State; Parliament may establish a common High Court for two or more States under Article 231.
Article 226 writ jurisdiction is wider than Article 32, as it can be invoked for enforcement of legal rights as well as fundamental rights.

static.mainsAngle: Examine the limits of judicial observations on matters of legislative policy, using the debate over the age of juvenility as an illustration.

static.topic: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Children and Juvenile Justice
static.whatIsIt: The JJ Act, 2015 governs children in conflict with law and children in need of care and protection; it treats a person below 18 as a child, while permitting 16–18 year olds accused of heinous offences to be tried as adults after assessment by the Juvenile Justice Board.
static.background: It replaced the Juvenile Justice Act, 2000, in the wake of the Justice Verma Committee report and public debate following the 2012 Delhi gang-rape case. The Act came into force in January 2016, and the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Amendment Act, 2021 strengthened adoption and district-level oversight provisions.
static.socioEconomic: Children in conflict with law overwhelmingly come from socio-economically disadvantaged backgrounds, so any move towards greater deterrence must be weighed against rehabilitation, education and reintegration outcomes.
static.whyInNews: The Kerala High Court's suggestion to reduce the juvenile age limit to 16 revives debate over the Act's age threshold and its special provision for 16–18 year olds accused of heinous offences.
static.wayForward: Strengthen Juvenile Justice Boards, after-care and rehabilitation infrastructure, and base any revision of the age threshold on empirical evidence rather than episodic public outrage.
keyTerms: Child in need of care and protection
prelimsPointers: The JJ Act, 2015 defines a 'heinous offence' as one for which the minimum punishment is imprisonment for seven years or more.

static.topic: Federalism & Centre-State Relations
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: India is a quasi-federal union in which legislative powers are divided by the Seventh Schedule into Union, State and Concurrent Lists, with residuary powers vested in the Union under Article 248.
static.background: Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2007) examined Centre-State balance. The Governor (Article 153) acts as the Centre's constitutional representative and has been a flashpoint over assent to Bills under Article 200 and reservation of Bills for the President under Article 201.
static.geography: India; the immediate context is Tamil Nadu's engagement with the Union government.
static.socioEconomic: Centre-State disputes affect state finances, education, health and welfare delivery, and can shape regional political demands.
static.whyInNews: Former bureaucrats have sought restoration of Tamil Nadu's high-level committee on Union-State relations, set up in April 2025 amid DMK-Centre tensions over delimitation, NEET and education.
static.wayForward: Revive and institutionalise regular Union-State consultative mechanisms, strengthen the Inter-State Council under Article 263, and resolve disputes through dialogue rather than unilateral action.
prelimsPointers: Concurrent List: union law prevails on repugnancy unless a state law is reserved for the President's assent under Article 254.
Inter-State Council under Article 263 is a recommendatory dispute-resolution body.
Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2007) examined Centre-State relations.
static.mainsAngle: Recent spats over Governor's assent and fiscal devolution — assess cooperative federalism in practice.

stories.headline: Congress units clash over Mekedatu dam as Cauvery dispute resurfaces
stories.summary: Karnataka's renewed advocacy of the Mekedatu balancing reservoir on the Cauvery has reopened a public rift within the Congress, with the party's Tamil Nadu unit criticising the Karnataka Chief Minister's push for the project. The Karnataka side has publicly dismissed that criticism, indicating it is 'least bothered' by the Tamil Nadu unit's position, even as Tamil Nadu's long-standing objection to additional storage across the river remains unchanged. The exchange revives the central fault line of the Cauvery dispute: Karnataka's claim to a share for drinking water and irrigation within its basin against Tamil Nadu's insistence on assured downstream flows for its delta. Because the dispute is governed by tribunal awards and Supreme Court directions rather than by ordinary politics, the row tests both federal comity and intra-party coordination within a national party that governs one of the states involved.
stories.whyItMatters: Inter-state river disputes are a standing GS-II federalism theme, and Cauvery is the standard case study for tribunal awards, Article 262 and the politics of water-sharing. The intra-party dimension also illustrates how regional identity can override party discipline.

perspectives.take: Frames the story as 'Congress vs Congress', foregrounding the internal contradiction of a national party whose Tamil Nadu unit is attacking a Congress Chief Minister in Karnataka over a river project.
Second report highlights the Karnataka Chief Minister's dismissive 'least bothered' response, framing the row as a deepening of the Cauvery rift rather than a purely intra-party squabble.

static.topic: Cauvery Water Dispute and Inter-State River Water Tribunals
static.syllabusNode: Federalism — Centre-State and Inter-State relations; mechanisms for dispute redressal
static.whatIsIt: A long-running water-sharing dispute among Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry over the Cauvery, adjudicated through the tribunal mechanism created by the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, which itself flows from Article 262 of the Constitution.
static.background: The Cauvery rises at Talakaveri in the Brahmagiri hills of Kodagu district, Karnataka, and drains a basin shared by Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry. Agreements of the colonial and early post-Independence period failed to settle shares, and the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal was constituted in 1990 under the ISRWD Act, 1956. The Tribunal gave its final award in 2007, allocating shares among the basin states; the Supreme Court modified the allocation in 2018 and directed the setting up of the Cauvery Water Management Authority to implement the award. Periodic distress years, when Karnataka is directed to release specified flows, have repeatedly triggered protests and litigation.
static.geography: The Cauvery is an east-flowing peninsular river, roughly 800 km long, rising in Karnataka and flowing through Tamil Nadu to the Bay of Bengal, with a delta that is among the most intensively irrigated regions in India. Its major tributaries include the Kabini, Hemavati, Amaravati, Bhavani and Noyyal. The basin is largely rain-fed and monsoon-dependent, making it acutely vulnerable to deficit years.
static.socioEconomic: The basin supports intensive paddy cultivation in the Tamil Nadu delta and significant irrigation and drinking-water needs in Karnataka, including for Bengaluru. Competing agricultural livelihoods, urban water demand and political mobilisation around language and region make any allocation decision highly sensitive.
static.whyInNews: Karnataka's renewed push for the Mekedatu project has drawn criticism from the Tamil Nadu unit of the Congress, and the Karnataka Chief Minister has publicly dismissed that criticism, reviving the dispute in the political domain.
static.wayForward: Strengthen the Cauvery Water Management Authority's technical capacity and data-sharing between basin states, institutionalise a distress-sharing formula for deficit years, and pursue basin-level water accounting and demand management rather than project-by-project contestation.
prelimsPointers: Article 262 empowers Parliament to provide for adjudication of inter-state river water disputes and to bar the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and other courts in such matters.
The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 provides for constitution of ad hoc tribunals; the Cauvery Tribunal was constituted in 1990 and gave its final award in 2007.
The Supreme Court modified the Cauvery allocation in 2018 and directed creation of the Cauvery Water Management Authority.
The Cauvery basin is shared by Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether the tribunal-based mechanism under Article 262 and the ISRWD Act, 1956 is adequate for resolving inter-state river disputes, using the Cauvery as a case study.

static.topic: Mekedatu Balancing Reservoir Project
static.syllabusNode: Infrastructure — water resources, dams and river basin development; also GS-I Geography of resources
static.whatIsIt: A proposed balancing reservoir across the Cauvery at Mekedatu in Ramanagara district, Karnataka, close to the Tamil Nadu border, intended to store monsoon flows for drinking water and power generation and to regulate releases downstream.
static.background: Karnataka has argued that a balancing reservoir would help it utilise its allocated share without violating the tribunal award, and would secure drinking water for Bengaluru. Tamil Nadu has consistently opposed the project on the ground that any new storage upstream would impair flows into its delta and that the proposal requires the concurrence of co-basin states and central clearances. The project has been the subject of repeated political flashpoints, litigation and statements by both state governments.
static.geography: Mekedatu lies on the Cauvery in Karnataka's Ramanagara district, upstream of the Tamil Nadu border, in a stretch where the river flows through a gorge. The site's proximity to the state boundary is central to Tamil Nadu's objection.
static.socioEconomic: Karnataka presents the project as a drinking-water and irrigation security measure for a rapidly growing urban region; Tamil Nadu presents it as a threat to the delta's farming economy and to the reliability of releases it is entitled to under the award.
static.whyInNews: The project has re-entered political discourse after the Karnataka Chief Minister's advocacy of it drew criticism from the Congress's Tamil Nadu unit, with the Karnataka side dismissing that criticism.
static.wayForward: Any movement on the project would require resolution of inter-state consent, statutory and environmental clearances, and a credible assurance mechanism on downstream flows — making basin-level negotiation preferable to unilateral positioning.
prelimsPointers: Mekedatu is a proposed balancing reservoir on the Cauvery in Ramanagara district, Karnataka, near the Tamil Nadu border.
Karnataka links the project to drinking water needs, including for Bengaluru, and to regulation of monsoon releases.
Tamil Nadu opposes new upstream storage on the ground that it would affect flows into the Cauvery delta.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how competing claims of upstream storage and downstream assurance can be reconciled within the framework of inter-state river water dispute adjudication.

prelims: Article 262 of the Constitution allows Parliament to legislate on adjudication of inter-state river water disputes and to exclude the jurisdiction of courts in such matters.
The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal was constituted in 1990 under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956; its final award came in 2007 and was modified by the Supreme Court in 2018.
The Cauvery basin is shared by Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry, with the river rising at Talakaveri in Karnataka's Kodagu district.
Mekedatu is a proposed balancing reservoir on the Cauvery in Karnataka's Ramanagara district, opposed by Tamil Nadu.
stories.mainsQuestion: Inter-state river water disputes are increasingly fought in the political domain rather than resolved through institutional mechanisms. Examine this in the context of the Cauvery dispute and suggest reforms to the tribunal-based framework under Article 262.
